newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada mum on speculation of role in Lima standoff.
newsitem.headline: Canada mum on speculation of role in Lima standoff.

text.p: Canada readily agreed to host the emergency hostage summit between Peru and Japan but there was speculation on Saturday that the country may yet be asked to play a much larger role.

Canadian officials will not confirm or deny media reports that, as a way of ending the hostage standoff, Canadian troops may be used to provide safe passage to Cuba for the Peruvian guerrillas holding 72 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima.
Canadian foreign affairs minister Lloyd Axworthy, who recently returned from a high-profile visit to Cuba, said in Ottawa on Friday that he could not comment on such speculation.

Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto also would not comment on the possibility of using Canadian troops at a news conference after his meeting with Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori on Saturday.

"At the present stage we cannot say what sort of ultimate solution will be realised," he said, adding that it would be counterproductive to disclose the range of options discussed at the summit meeting.
Both leaders, however, praised the involvement of Canada's ambassador to Peru, Anthony Vincent, and said he would play an important role in the new talks planned with the rebels.

Vincent was initially taken hostage in the Dec. 17 storming of the Lima embassy, but was released by the Tupac Amaru rebels to help open up talks with the Peruvian government in the early stages of the crisis.

Fujimori said Vincent, a member of an international commission mediating between Peru and the rebels, has the confidence of both governments. "He is an outstanding, very important pipeline for discussions and he can surely contribute very importantly to the solution of the problem."

Canada's ambassador to Cuba, Mark Entwistle, was staying at the same downtown Toronto hotel where the Peruvian-Japanese talks were being held. But a spokesman for Canada's foreign affairs department said it was a coincidence that Entwistle was there and that he was on a cross-country speaking tour and not involved in the talks.

Canadian government officials have said they saw their role in the Toronto talks as more of a facilitator than a mediator. But the country has a long history of sending in peackeeping troops to help defuse international crises.
